title: Mobile / iPad app — flow inspiration
intro: Complete phone and iPad flows for running a live simulation session without a desktop: recording control, filling a checklist, timers, learner tagging, dictated notes, intercom, the sim tech's room check and private debrief annotations. Focus is the device-native experience (live state, lock screen, one-hand, big targets) and iPad layouts; the desktop/SRV side is in 04-recording and the QR phone remote in 08-debrief-review. Sources: Mobbin (all flows shown) and Refero (searched, but its image CDN refused the downloads, so no Refero flow made the report). Researched 2026-09-30.
baseline: Today TouchPro is LearningSpace's only tablet client and there is no phone app. The solution concept (2026-09-10) proposes a QR-scan checklist, remote start/stop recording, private debrief annotations, a sim-tech setup checklist, a timer (customers buy separate digital timers today), learner tagging, timestamped speech-to-text notes and the phone as an intercom microphone. Constraints: a web page is preferred for the debrief page, phones may be banned in summative exams, tablets must not be mandated, and no biometrics tied to names may go to the cloud. Leadership wants to see which jobs genuinely benefit from mobile before committing to an MVP.

jobs.title: Recording control
jobs.description: Remote start/stop, recording-state indicator, which room/camera, confirmation, lock-screen / live activity / widget controls

jobs.title: Checklist interface
jobs.description: Fill a checklist/rubric fast during a live event: big toggles, partial credit, comments, auto-timestamp, offline, submit/review

jobs.title: Timer
jobs.description: Session/phase timers, multiple timers, visible across the room, alerts, lock-screen/live activity

jobs.title: Learner tagging
jobs.description: Pick who's in the session or who did what: roster chips, quick-add, QR/badge scan, attach a tag to a moment

jobs.title: Speech-to-text note taking
jobs.description: Dictate a note that's timestamped to the recording; edit transcript; on-device vs. cloud transcription indicator

jobs.title: Intercom device
jobs.description: Push-to-talk to a room or device; target selection; muted/live state

jobs.title: Equipment check
jobs.description: Tech's pre-session setup checklist per room: scan QR on the room, tick items, flag missing/broken, hand off

jobs.title: Debriefing tool: annotations
jobs.description: Private timestamped annotations/bookmarks during playback, controlling the big screen from the device

products.name: GoPro Quik
products.why: The phone as a remote for a camera: storage and battery before you start, a record button that morphs into stop, and a one-thumb HiLight bookmark beside stop.

products.name: Luma
products.why: Door-side QR check-in: confirm the person on a sheet, get a success toast while the scanner stays open, and undo a wrong check-in.

products.name: Otter AI
products.why: Every paragraph and every comment carries a speaker and timestamp chip, and playback stays docked above the keyboard while you correct the transcript.

products.name: Toggl Track
products.why: Named phase timers with full-screen digits, separate Stop (pause) and End session intents, and one-tap restart from history.

products.name: Forest
products.why: The clearest case for a phone timer: remaining time and phase on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island, with one stop control, without opening the app.

products.name: Slack
products.why: Push-to-talk as an explicit mode, with a huge hold-to-speak target and a muted state shown in two places.

products.name: Amazon Alexa
products.why: Separates a live two-way Drop In from a one-way Announce, behind an explicit opt-in: two different intercom intents most tools merge.

products.name: Google TV
products.why: Driving a big screen from the phone: a docked bar that names the connected screen and ±30s skips; its five-step Wi-Fi pairing is the counter-example to QR pairing.

products.name: Lifesum
products.why: A scored assessment filled one item at a time with full-row targets, a slider for graded answers and a score breakdown at the end; also shows the cost of 41 items.

products.name: Zoom
products.why: Admitting people from a waiting-room toast, a participant count on the toolbar and an explicit connecting-to-audio state before you can be heard. No recording control is shown.

products.name: Fabric
products.why: Frame drawings saved as timestamped comments and a big Stop/Resume voice note with transcript tabs, but no on-device indicator; its tiny checkbox list is a counter-example.

products.name: Journal
products.why: Recording state on the lock screen (waveform, timer, one stop control; no pause) and an in-app recorder where Done stays disabled until you pause.

products.name: American Airlines
products.why: One readiness hub per event with time-gated tasks (what you can do now vs. not yet), but no pass/fail or flag states.

products.name: Yuka
products.why: Flagging a problem on a recently scanned item: pick a category, attach a mandatory photo (Send stays disabled without it), get a thank-you with a response time.

patterns.title: One unmistakable record state, and bookmark with the same thumb
patterns.body: GoPro Quik shows remaining storage and battery before you start, morphs the record button into a stop square, keeps a red dot and elapsed time visible, and puts a HiLight button next to stop with a full-screen 'tagged' confirmation. That combines recording control with a one-tap timestamped marker, which is exactly what faculty need while walking the room. Journal keeps the recording state alive on the lock screen. Neither shows which room or camera is being controlled, which Essentials must add.

patterns.title: The timer lives outside the app, but only natively
patterns.body: Forest puts remaining time, the phase name and a single stop control on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island, and Toggl offers full-screen digits for across-the-room reading. This is the strongest evidence in the module that a job benefits from a phone rather than the SRV. It is also native-only: a web client or a phone-banned exam gets none of it, so a large in-app full-screen timer is the fallback that must work everywhere.

patterns.title: Named phases, pause ≠ end, restart from history
patterns.body: Toggl separates Stop (pause the clock) from End session (finish the cycle), flips colour and label when the phase changes, and asks before skipping a phase. Its timer list lets you restart any named timer with one tap. Simulation phases (briefing, scenario, debrief) repeat every session, so restart-from-history beats configuring a new countdown each time.

patterns.title: Confirm the person, then stay ready for the next one
patterns.body: Luma shows a confirmation sheet (name, status, ticket) before checking someone in, then returns straight to the scanner with a success toast and offers Undo. Zoom admits people from a waiting-room toast and keeps a participant count on the toolbar. Both treat 'who is in the session' as a fast, reversible stream at the door, not a roster form, which is the case for tagging learners on a phone.

patterns.title: Every note carries its timestamp chip
patterns.body: Otter pins a timestamp chip to each comment and a speaker-plus-time stamp to each transcript paragraph; Fabric saves frame drawings as 'Drawing · 00:00:00' entries and keeps a timestamp chip on the reply field. Fabric's voice note diverges: its transcript has no per-line timestamps, so text can't be traced back to a moment. None of the flows shows an on-device versus cloud transcription indicator.

patterns.title: Talking into a room is a mode, with live and muted always visible
patterns.body: Slack makes push-to-talk an explicit mode with a huge hold target and shows muted state on both your tile and the control. Alexa separates a live Drop In from a one-way Announce behind an opt-in. Zoom shows 'connecting to audio' before you can be heard. For a phone that talks into a live sim room, the risk is an open mic, so hold-to-talk plus a persistent live/muted state is the default to copy.

patterns.title: Name the screen you are driving; pairing must be one step
patterns.body: Google TV's remote keeps a docked bar naming the connected screen and offers ±30s skips, which suits jumping between debrief moments. Getting there takes five steps of Wi-Fi/Bluetooth discovery, which fails a faculty member in a debrief room. Keep the named-screen bar and coarse transport, but pair by QR as 08-debrief-review proposes.

patterns.title: One big item at a time beats a checkbox list
patterns.body: Lifesum fills a scored assessment one item per screen with full-row targets, keeps Next disabled until an answer is picked, uses a slider for graded answers and ends with a score breakdown. Fabric's standard small checkboxes fail gloved, one-handed use. American Airlines groups readiness into one hub with time-gated tasks but has no pass/fail states. The live checklist needs Lifesum's targets and review step without its 41-item length.

open_questions: No iPad flows. Mobbin's search API has no iPad filter and every shortlisted flow is a phone layout (the only tablet layout found, Superlist, is a generic list-detail view). The tablet-vs-phone question from stakeholders is not answered here; it needs a manual pass through Mobbin's iPad catalogue or an audit of TouchPro.

The strongest mobile wins (lock-screen timer, Live Activity recording, background push-to-talk) are native-only. A web-first debrief page and phone bans in summative exams mean they cannot be the MVP surface. Which jobs justify a native app, and does each have a web or tablet fallback?

Equipment check has no end-to-end reference: nothing shows scanning a room QR, ticking items pass/fail, flagging a broken item and handing off. The flow has to be assembled from Luma's scan-and-confirm, Lifesum's big-target items, American Airlines' readiness hub and Yuka's per-item problem report with a mandatory photo.
No flow shows an on-device versus cloud transcription indicator, which GDPR makes a requirement for speech-to-text notes. This has to be designed without a reference.

Live rubrics: Lifesum shows that 41 one-at-a-time items are too slow for a live scenario. How long are real OSCE checklists, and do they need sections, a grid on tablet, or partial scoring after the session?

Learner tagging is covered for who is present (Luma, Zoom) but not for who did what: only GoPro's HiLight shows tagging a moment, with no person attached. Refero was searched but its image CDN returned HTTP 403, so no Refero flows could be included.
